title: Godliness with Contentment, and the Good Fight
summary: Paul instructs slaves to honor their masters so that the gospel is not discredited, then exposes the false teachers as conceited, quarrelsome, and eager to use religion for profit. Godliness with contentment is great gain, he says, while the desire to be rich leads to ruin, since the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. He charges Timothy to flee these things, pursue righteousness, and fight the good fight of the faith, and he tells the rich to be generous and to hope in God. The letter ends with a final plea to guard what has been entrusted.
story: This is the last chapter of 1 Timothy, and it gathers up the letter's concerns. The section on groups within the church, which began in 5:1, closes with slaves (verses 1-2). Then Paul returns to the false teachers with whom he began in chapter 1, adding a new charge: they treat godliness as a way to make money. The theme of wealth carries through the rest of the chapter, broken by a solemn charge to Timothy and a burst of praise to God. The letter ends where it started, with the deposit of truth that Timothy must guard against empty talk and so-called knowledge.
historical:
Slavery was woven into the economy of the Roman Empire. Estimates vary, but a substantial share of the population of cities like Ephesus was enslaved, and slaves worked as household servants, laborers, craftsmen, teachers, doctors, and managers. Slavery in the Roman world was not based on race; people became slaves through war, debt, birth to a slave mother, or abandonment as infants, and many were freed during their lifetimes. Churches included both slaves and masters, sometimes in the same household, which raised new questions about how believers who were brothers in Christ should relate within an unequal institution.

The charge in verse 13 recalls that Christ Jesus “made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.” Pilate was the Roman prefect who governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, and his name was fixed in the church's memory as the official under whom Jesus was crucified; it later entered the Apostles' Creed. The title “King of kings and Lord of lords” (verse 15) had been used by rulers in the ancient Near East, and in the Roman period emperors received lavish divine titles. Paul gives the title to God alone, who “alone is immortal” (verse 16).
cultural:
Traveling teachers in the Greco-Roman world often charged fees, and some philosophers were mocked as sellers of wisdom who were in it for the money. Paul's opponents seem to have fit that pattern, treating their teaching as a means of gain (verse 5). Moral philosophers of the time, especially the Stoics and Cynics, praised self-sufficiency (autarkeia), the freedom that comes from needing little. Paul uses the same word but gives it a different ground: contentment rests not in the self but in God, who provides food and clothing, and in the knowledge that we brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out of it (verse 7, echoing Job 1:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:15).

Wealthy believers in Ephesus would have been expected, by the customs of their city, to act as benefactors, funding public buildings, festivals, and meals in return for public honor and inscriptions. Paul redirects that expectation: the rich are to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share, storing up treasure for the age to come rather than honor in this one (verses 17-19). The title “man of God” (verse 11) was used in the Old Testament of Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, and other prophets, and places Timothy in that line of those who speak for God.
literary: The chapter moves in five steps. Verses 1-2 finish the instructions to groups in the church. Verses 3-10 describe the false teachers and their love of money, ending with the proverb-like saying of verse 10. Verses 11-16 turn sharply with “But you, O man of God” to a charge built on paired commands (flee and pursue, fight and take hold) and climax in a doxology, a formal ascription of praise, that piles up titles for God. Verses 17-19 return to wealth, now addressing believers who are rich. Verses 20-21 close the letter with a final charge and a short blessing. Notice how the chapter plays on the idea of gain: the false teachers seek profit from godliness, but godliness with contentment is itself great gain, and the rich are to lay hold of what is truly life.

outline.t: False teachers who treat godliness as gain
Godliness with contentment; the love of money
Flee, pursue, fight: the charge to the man of God

doctrines.note: Contentment is a form of wisdom: we bring nothing into the world and take nothing out, and food and clothing are enough. The desire to be rich is a trap that leads to “ruin and destruction” (verse 9).

God is “the blessed and only Sovereign One,” who alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light (verses 15-16). He is also the one “who richly provides all things for us to enjoy” (verse 17): majestic beyond reach and generous beyond measure.

Timothy is to keep the commandment until “the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 14), and the rich are to store up a foundation for the future. The coming age puts present wealth in its place.

words.note: Autarkeia, contentment or self-sufficiency. The word was a watchword of Stoic and Cynic philosophers for the freedom of needing little. Paul uses it for a contentment grounded in God rather than in the self (compare Philippians 4:11-13, where he uses the related adjective).

Philarguria, love of money, literally fondness for silver. Found only here in the New Testament, though a related adjective describes the Pharisees in Luke 16:14. The verse does not say money is evil, or that it is the only root of evil, but that the love of it is a root from which every kind of evil can grow.

Parathēkē, a deposit, something entrusted to another for safekeeping. In the ancient world a deposit left with a trusted person had to be returned intact. Timothy is to guard the gospel entrusted to him (verse 20), a theme 2 Timothy develops (2 Timothy 1:12-14).

Gnōsis, knowledge. In verse 20 Paul speaks of what is falsely called knowledge, apparently the opponents' own claim to superior insight. In the later second century, Irenaeus took this phrase as the title of his great work against those later called Gnostics.

christ: The chapter presents Christ as both example and coming king. He “made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate” (verse 13), standing firm before the power of Rome, and Timothy's own confession is to be made in that light. The command must be kept until “the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 14), and God will bring that appearing about in his own time. The sound words of the Lord Jesus Christ are the standard for all teaching (verse 3). Jesus also taught that no one can serve both God and money (Matthew 6:24) and that treasure is to be stored in heaven (Matthew 6:19-21); verses 17-19 apply that teaching to the wealthy members of the church. The Lord who had nowhere to lay his head is the pattern of godliness with contentment.

hard.q: Why does Paul tell slaves to honor their masters instead of condemning slavery?
hard.a:
Modern readers rightly find these verses troubling, knowing the horrors of slavery and the use of such texts to defend the Atlantic slave trade. Several things are worth saying. Paul addresses believers living within a system they had no power to abolish; a small, suspected movement calling for slave revolt would have been crushed, and the gospel discredited (verse 1). His concern is that God's name and the teaching not be blasphemed. At the same time, the New Testament planted principles that undermined slavery from within: masters and slaves are brothers (verse 2; Philemon 16), masters are accountable to the same Lord (Ephesians 6:9), slave traders are listed among lawbreakers (1:10), and, on the most common reading of a disputed verse, Paul urges slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21).

Christians have differed on how to weigh this. Some stress that the New Testament's silence on abolition reflects a limited horizon that later Christians rightly moved beyond, guided by the gospel's own logic. Others stress that its approach, transforming relationships from within rather than attacking the institution directly, was wise in its setting and finally bore fruit in Christian abolitionist movements. Both agree that nothing here endorses the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, which was built on kidnapping, the very act 1:10 condemns.

questions: Paul says godliness with contentment is great gain. What makes contentment so hard in a culture built on wanting more?
Timothy is told to flee some things and pursue others. What do you most need to flee, and what do you most need to pursue?
If you count yourself among the rich of this present age, as most people in wealthy nations are by global standards, what would it look like to be rich in good works and ready to share?
